common_name: Sweet Caroline Bronze Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Bronze-Purple Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the Sweet Caroline series was bred with a more compact, less rampant habit than older ornamental sweet potato vines, making it easier to keep in bounds in mixed containers.

directions: Sweet Caroline Bronze produces deeply lobed, ivy-like leaves in a warm bronze-purple, a softer, more finely cut alternative to the broad near-black leaves of the older cultivar Blackie, on a plant bred to be more compact and manageable in containers than earlier ornamental sweet potato vine selections. Its trailing stems cascade over pot edges and retaining walls, and the finely lobed foliage texture pairs well with both bold tropical companions and fine-textured annuals in a mixed planting. Give it well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like other ornamental sweet potato vines it is extremely heat-tolerant and grows fastest in the peak of Gulf South summer, needing only occasional trimming to keep it in scale.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Light Green Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Chartreuse Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the compact Sweet Caroline habit fits smaller container combinations better than the more vigorous, rambling growth of older chartreuse ornamental sweet potato vine cultivars like Margarita.

directions: Sweet Caroline Light Green carries bright chartreuse-green, deeply lobed foliage on a more compact, restrained vine than older lime-colored sweet potato vine cultivars, making it easier to keep proportionate in a mixed container rather than letting one plant take over the whole pot. The luminous foliage color brightens shaded corners and pairs naturally with cool blue and purple flowering companions or bold dark-leaved foliage plants for contrast. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates a bit more shade than most chartreuse foliage plants while still holding good color, and needs only occasional trimming to control its trailing spread through the heat of summer.

common_name: Illusion Emerald Lace Sweet Potato Vine (Finely Cut Lacy-Leaf Ornamental Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the finely dissected foliage of the Illusion series gives a much softer, ferny texture than broad-leaved ornamental sweet potato vine cultivars.

directions: Illusion Emerald Lace stands apart from most ornamental sweet potato vine cultivars for its finely dissected, almost ferny bright green leaves, a delicate lacy texture that reads very differently from the broad, heart-shaped or lobed leaves of cultivars like Margarita or Blackie. The airy foliage trails and cascades over container edges without the visual heaviness of larger-leaved selections, making it a useful filler texture in mixed plantings alongside bolder companions. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it is just as heat-tolerant and fast-growing as other ornamental sweet potato vines through the peak of Gulf South summer, needing only occasional trimming to keep it in scale.

common_name: Superbells Blue Calibrachoa (Trailing Violet-Blue Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring as soon as hard freeze danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February-March for spring bloom. Calibrachoa needs excellent drainage and acidic potting mix (pH 5.5-6.0); alkaline conditions cause iron-deficiency chlorosis. It is not grown from seed — all Superbells calibrachoa are vegetatively propagated to maintain the cultivar.

directions: Superbells Blue produces hundreds of small, one-inch, petunia-like flowers in a rich violet-blue over trailing stems that cascade over container edges, one of the most classic and widely grown colors in the Superbells series. Like other calibrachoa it is self-cleaning, dropping spent flowers without leaving behind dried, browning petals that need deadheading, so the plant needs only regular watering and fertilizing to maintain nonstop bloom through its cool-season peak. Plant in full sun in well-drained, acidic potting mix or garden soil, and feed regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer, since calibrachoa is a heavy feeder that declines quickly in alkaline conditions; expect the heaviest bloom in the cooler shoulder seasons, with a slowdown during peak Gulf South summer heat.

common_name: Superbells Coralberry Punch Calibrachoa (Trailing Coral-Pink Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring as soon as hard freeze danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February-March for spring bloom. Calibrachoa needs excellent drainage and acidic potting mix (pH 5.5-6.0); alkaline conditions cause iron-deficiency chlorosis. It is not grown from seed — all Superbells calibrachoa are vegetatively propagated to maintain the cultivar.

directions: Superbells Coralberry Punch produces small, petunia-like flowers in a vivid coral-pink with a subtly darker throat, adding a warm punch of color to hanging baskets and container edges over trailing stems that spread and cascade through the growing season. It shares the self-cleaning habit of the rest of the Superbells series, dropping spent flowers cleanly so the plant looks tidy without deadheading, and needs only regular watering and feeding to sustain its long bloom period. Plant in full sun in well-drained, acidic potting mix, feeding regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer, and expect the strongest flowering during the cooler parts of the season, with some slowdown during the most intense Gulf South summer heat.
